title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
short: Islamic tradition credits the caliph ʿUthmān (c. 650); some scholars place closure under ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ḥajjāj (c. 700) or later. Manuscript evidence is now testing these positions.

needs.ask: Align early manuscript transcriptions from Corpus Coranicum verse by verse, coding each difference as orthographic, consonantal or verse division, and test single-archetype and fluid-text stemmata.
Build a model combining the radiocarbon dates of early Qurʾān parchments with palaeographic evidence to bound when the Uthmanic archetype was produced.
Image the Sanaa palimpsest and other dispersed early fragments so that the erased lower text and unpublished leaves can be read and transcribed.

matters: The date at which the consonantal skeleton (rasm) was fixed determines how far the text can be used as evidence for the first decades of Islam, how its relation to Muhammad's preaching is assessed, and how the early caliphate's religious authority is understood. A mid-seventh-century closure supports reading the Qurʾān as a near-contemporary witness; a Marwanid or later closure would allow for substantial editorial shaping during the conquest period. The question also bears on the history of Arabic orthography and on the reliability of the Islamic tradition's accounts of collection.
stuck: The earliest manuscripts are fragmentary, undated, dispersed across collections and often published only in part, and the Sanaa lower text survives as an erased palimpsest. Radiocarbon dates give the death of the animal whose skin became parchment, not the date of writing, and their ranges often span several decades on either side of 650 and 700. The literary accounts of ʿUthmān's and al-Ḥajjāj's interventions were recorded later and are read differently by scholars with different views of the tradition's reliability.
solved: A published stemmatic analysis of all variants in the dated and datable manuscripts (including the Sanaa lower text and the regional-codex variants), using shared orthographic errors to test whether the surviving Uthmanic-type manuscripts descend from a single written archetype, combined with a radiocarbon and palaeographic model that bounds when that archetype was produced, with results reproducible from open data.
approach: The manuscript work of Déroche (2009), Déroche (2014) and Cellard (2018), the studies of the Sanaa lower text by Sadeghi (2010), Sadeghi (2012) and Hilali (2017), and the stemmatic arguments of Cook (2004), van Putten (2019) and Sidky (2020) already supply most of the method. The open question is how their results combine with the radiocarbon dates and with the later dating defended by Wansbrough (1977) and Shoemaker (2022).

Transcriptions of early manuscripts from Corpus Coranicum and published editions can be aligned verse by verse, with each difference coded as orthographic (spelling conventions, scriptio defectiva), consonantal or a matter of verse division. Keeping these categories separate matters, since shared orthographic idiosyncrasies are the evidence van Putten (2019) used for a single written archetype.

Phylogenetic and stemmatic methods, of the kind Sidky (2020) applied and Fedeli (2020) has discussed for digital editions, can then test rival models: a single Uthmanic archetype copied into regional exemplars, several independent sources later merged, or a text still fluid until the Marwanid reforms. Each predicts a different pattern of shared errors and spelling conventions across manuscripts of different regions and dates.

A tested stemma of the Uthmanic manuscripts, with the regional variants reported in the literary tradition mapped onto it, would be useful in its own right, whatever the date of closure. The Sanaa lower text would sit outside it as a check on how a non-Uthmanic tradition behaves.

Linking the same dataset to radiocarbon results (Marx 2019), palaeographic classes and the Mingana Collection and Tübingen dates would test whether manuscripts placed early by the stemma are also early by carbon. Given calibration ranges and the interval between preparing parchment and writing on it, as Shoemaker (2022) stresses, the date of standardization will probably stay a range of decades, though one that might exclude some positions argued by Sinai (2014) and his critics.

All of this depends on custodians and laboratories: publication and imaging of fragments held at Dār al-Makhṭūṭāt in Sanaa and elsewhere, multispectral imaging of palimpsests, and further radiocarbon dating. Specialists in Qurʾānic manuscripts would need to review every alignment and variant classification.

existing.title: Quranic Studies: Sources and Methods of Scriptural Interpretation
existing.venue: London Oriental Series 31. Oxford: Oxford University Press
existing.note: Argued from form-critical analysis that the canonical text emerged gradually and was not fixed until around 800.

existing.title: The Stemma of the Regional Codices of the Koran
existing.note: Showed that the variants reported for the regional codices form a coherent stemma consistent with copies made from a single exemplar, as the tradition about ʿUthmān describes.

existing.title: La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus
existing.note: Codicological, orthographic and textual study of one of the oldest large Qurʾān manuscripts, showing a rasm close to the standard text with orthographic variation.

existing.title: The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet
existing.note: Analysed the non-Uthmanic lower text of the Sanaa palimpsest and reported a radiocarbon date for one of its leaves placing the parchment before about 671.

existing.title: Ṣanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān
existing.note: Edited the lower text of several palimpsest folios and argued that it represents an independent textual tradition, while the Uthmanic text derives from a single archetype.

existing.title: Qur'ans of the Umayyads: A First Overview
existing.note: Surveyed Umayyad-period manuscripts and discussed Marwanid interventions in script, orthography and book production.

existing.title: When did the consonantal skeleton of the Quran reach closure? Part I
existing.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 77 (2): 273–292
existing.note: Weighed the literary, documentary and manuscript evidence and argued that closure before the Marwanid period is more probable (Part II in BSOAS 77 (3): 509–521).

existing.authors: University of Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library
existing.title: Birmingham Qur'an manuscript dated among the oldest in the world
existing.venue: University of Birmingham news release, 22 July 2015
existing.note: Announced Oxford radiocarbon dating of the Mingana 1572a leaves to 568–645 CE at 95.4 per cent probability.

existing.title: The Sanaa Palimpsest: The Transmission of the Qur'an in the First Centuries AH
existing.venue: Oxford: Oxford University Press, in association with the Institute of Ismaili Studies (Qur'anic Studies Series 17)
existing.note: Edition and study of DAM 01-27.1 that reads the lower text as possibly a teaching or exercise text rather than a complete rival codex.

existing.title: Codex Amrensis 1
existing.note: Reconstruction and edition of an early Hijazi-script codex whose leaves are dispersed among several collections.

existing.title: "The Grace of God" as evidence for a written Uthmanic archetype: the importance of shared orthographic idiosyncrasies
existing.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 82 (2): 271–288
existing.note: Showed that early manuscripts share arbitrary spelling conventions that are best explained by descent from one written archetype.

existing.authors: Michael Josef Marx and Tobias J. Jocham
existing.title: Radiocarbon (14C) Dating of Qurʾān Manuscripts
existing.venue: In A. Kaplony and M. Marx (eds.), Qurʾān Quotations Preserved on Papyrus Documents, 7th–10th Centuries (Leiden: Brill): 188–221
existing.note: Reported and discussed the Corpus Coranicum radiocarbon programme for early Qurʾān manuscripts and its interpretive limits.

existing.title: On the Regionality of Qurʾānic Codices
existing.venue: Journal of the International Qur'anic Studies Association 5: 133–210
existing.note: Matched variants in early manuscripts to the regional codices described in the tradition, supporting a stemma of regionally distributed copies.

existing.title: Digital Humanities and Qur'ānic Manuscript Studies: New Perspectives and Challenges for Collaborative Spaces and Plural Views
existing.venue: Journal of College of Sharia and Islamic Studies 38 (1)
existing.note: Reviews digital imaging, text encoding and phylogenetic approaches to early Qurʾān manuscripts, and the need for collaborative editions.

existing.title: Quranic Arabic: From its Hijazi Origins to its Classical Reading Traditions
existing.note: Linguistic reconstruction of the language of the rasm from early manuscripts and reading traditions.

existing.title: Creating the Qur'an: A Historical-Critical Study
existing.note: Argued for standardization under ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ḥajjāj and questioned the reliability of radiocarbon dates for fixing the text earlier.

archives.collection: DAM 01-27.1 (Ṣanʿāʾ 1 palimpsest) and other Qurʾān fragments found in the Great Mosque of Sanaa in 1972
archives.note: Holds the palimpsest whose lower text is the main non-Uthmanic witness; imaging from the 1980s–2000s exists but much remains unpublished, and access has been limited by the war in Yemen.

holdings.name: Ṣanʿāʾ palimpsest (Codex Ṣanʿāʾ 1)
holdings.note: Palimpsest whose erased lower text departs from the Uthmanic consonantal text; the principal non-standard early witness.

archives.repository: Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham
archives.collection: Mingana Collection, Islamic Arabic 1572a (Birmingham Qurʾān leaves)
archives.note: Two leaves radiocarbon dated in 2015; considered part of the same manuscript as leaves in BnF Arabe 328(c).

holdings.name: Birmingham Qurʾān leaves
holdings.note: Two Hijazi parchment leaves (parts of suras 18 to 20), radiocarbon dated in 2015 to 568-645 CE at 95.4 percent; assigned to the same codex as BnF Arabe 328(c).

archives.collection: Arabe 328 (Codex Parisino-petropolitanus and associated fragments) and other early Hijazi and Kufic fragments
archives.note: Early Qurʾān fragments available through Gallica; the remaining leaves of the Parisino-petropolitanus are in the National Library of Russia, St Petersburg.

holdings.name: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus, Paris part
holdings.note: The larger Paris portion of the Hijazi codex whose remaining leaves are in St Petersburg; dated palaeographically to the third quarter of the first Islamic century by Déroche (2009).

holdings.name: Qurʾān leaves, Arabe 328(c)
holdings.note: Sixteen leaves once bound with Arabe 328(a)-(b), now matched with the two Birmingham leaves of Islamic Arabic 1572a.

archives.note: Fully digitized fragment radiocarbon dated to 649–675 CE through the Coranica project.

holdings.name: Kufic Qurʾān fragment
holdings.note: Fully digitized fragment radiocarbon dated to 649-675 CE with over 95 percent probability.

archives.repository: Corpus Coranicum, Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities
archives.collection: Manuscripta Coranica database of early manuscripts, variant readings (Variae Lectiones) and radiocarbon results
archives.note: Open database with images, transliterations and metadata for many early Qurʾān manuscripts, the main platform for systematic comparison.

holdings.name: Manuscripta Coranica database
holdings.note: Images, transcriptions and metadata for early Qurʾān manuscripts, the base for aligning variants across witnesses.
